qs.q: A 44-year-old woman with severe iron-deficiency anaemia secondary to menorrhagia is scheduled for an elective hysterectomy in 5 days. Her Hb is 9.5 g/dL. What is the most appropriate intervention to correct her anaemia?
o: Give IV iron like ferric carboxymaltose
qs.e: When time is short before surgery or oral iron is not well tolerated, IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred to rapidly correct anaemia. Oral iron takes weeks to months and would not be optimal given the 5-day timeline.

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, and pelvic pain before the onset of menstruation. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, globular uterus with a thickened wall due to reactive myometrial hypertrophy. Microscopic examination demonstrates nests of endometrial stroma and glands deep within the myometrium between muscle bundles. Why do these ectopic glands fail to
o: They derive from the stratum basalis and do not undergo cyclic bleeding
They are destroyed by myometrial smooth muscle enzymes
They are constantly exposed to high systemic levels of progesterone
qs.e: In adenomyosis, the glands derive from the stratum basalis of the endometrium and do not undergo cyclic bleeding, unlike functional endometrial tissue in endometriosis. Progesterone and estrogen receptors are still present in these basal-derived nests.

qs.q: A 35-year-old nulliparous Black woman presents with menorrhagia and a dragging pelvic sensation. Ultrasound reveals multiple sharply circumscribed, firm, grey-white tumors with a whorled cut surface located entirely within the myometrium. What is the most common location of these benign smooth muscle tumors?
qs.e: Intramural leiomyomas are located within the myometrium and represent the most common site for these benign smooth muscle tumors. Submucosal fibroids are less frequent though more likely to cause significant uterine bleeding.

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe menorrhagia and fatigue. Laboratory investigations reveal microcytic hypochromic red cells, reduced serum ferritin, and decreased transferrin saturation. Which finding would you also expect in this iron deficiency state?
o: Normal iron stores reflected by ferritin
qs.e: Iron deficiency anaemia characteristically presents with an increased total iron-binding capacity alongside low serum iron and depleted ferritin stores. A decreased TIBC is seen in chronic disease states.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with 10‑day heavy periods and Hb 8 g/dL. What is your immediate management? — Stabilise with iron, give tranexamic acid, and arrange ultrasound if possible.
How would you differentiate menorrhagia due to fibroids from hormonal dysfunction without imaging? — Look for a palpable enlarged uterus, dysmenorrhoea, and a history of progressive worsening.

Why is tranexamic acid preferred over high‑dose estrogen in a patient with HIV on protease inhibitors? — Tranexamic acid has no drug‑interaction risk, while estrogen increases thrombotic risk in this population.

A patient with severe menorrhagia is found to have a normal PT/INR but a prolonged aPTT. What does this suggest and how do you proceed? — Possible intrinsic pathway defect; order factor assays or give desmopressin if bleeding is severe.
What are the red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral? — Hb <7 g/dL, hemodynamic instability, suspicion of malignancy, or failure of medical therapy after 24 h.
Explain why a levonorgestrel IUS may be unsuitable for a woman with active pelvic infection. — The device can exacerbate infection and is contraindicated until infection resolves.
In a low‑resource setting without ferritin testing, how would you assess iron deficiency? — Look for microcytic hypochromic anaemia on CBC, clinical pallor, and dietary history.
What is the rationale for avoiding combined oral contraceptives in a patient with uncontrolled hypertension? — Estrogen raises blood pressure and increases stroke risk.
ai.title: Menorrhagia
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding defined by objective loss or impact on quality of life. Recognise causes, assess severity, and manage with limited resources in low‑resource settings.

b: Prevalence 10‑20 % of women of reproductive age
Can lead to iron‑deficiency anaemia, infertility, and reduced quality of life
Determine location: uterine (structural, hormonal) vs systemic (coagulopathy, anemia)
sections.p: Assess severity, identify reversible causes, and consider local factors such as infections, nutrition, and traditional medicines.

b: Anaemia (Hb <10 g/dL) predicts need for urgent intervention
Uncontrolled bleeding can precipitate cardiac decompensation in patients with rheumatic heart disease
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, delayed diagnosis often results in severe anaemia requiring transfusion, which may be scarce.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues: pallor, tachycardia, and history of easy bruising suggest anaemia or coagulopathy.

t.b: Is the patient anaemic? – Low Hb confirms blood loss; microcytosis suggests iron deficiency
Is iron store depleted? – Ferritin <30 µg/L indicates iron deficiency
Is there early pregnancy? – Positive test changes management (avoid hormonal therapy)
Is there a structural lesion? – Detects fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis

t.a: Coagulation screen (PT/INR, aPTT) if bleeding disorder suspected
t.b: Is a coagulopathy present? – Prolonged values suggest factor deficiency or anticoagulant use
Are there infections influencing bleeding or treatment? – Positive results affect drug choice

b: Iron supplementation (oral ferrous sulfate) – restores iron stores; avoid if severe malabsorption
Combined oral contraceptive pill (COC) – stabilises endometrium; avoid in uncontrolled hypertension, active thromboembolism, or HIV on protease inhibitors
Levonorgestrel‑releasing intrauterine system (LNG‑IUS) – highly effective, long‑acting; consider cost and availability
Surgical options (myomectomy, endometrial ablation) – reserved for refractory cases; require referral
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, correct anaemia, and control bleeding. Use affordable, widely available drugs.

b: DUB: abnormal bleeding without structural lesion; often hormonal imbalance
Uterine rupture: severe pain, hemodynamic collapse, usually postpartum or after surgery
sections.p: Distinguish menorrhagia from dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) and from acute uterine rupture.

b: Acute phase response can raise ferritin falsely
Pregnancy can mask anaemia severity due to plasma volume expansion
sections.p: Normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency if inflammation is present; rely on clinical picture.

b: Ask about number of pads/tampons used and saturation level
Check for signs of chronic disease (e.g., TB, HIV) that may affect bleeding
Know first‑line oral therapy and when to refer for surgery
sections.p: Focus on history, impact on daily life, and anaemia signs. Be ready to discuss management in settings without labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia (tachycardia, dizziness)
Bleeding not controlled after 24 h of medical therapy
Suspicion of uterine rupture or malignancy
